Retention cohorts, basket width & a 5th-order milestone program¶

Question. Do customers who buy from many departments early come back more, and would free delivery on the 5th order pay for itself? Data. Instacart Online Grocery Shopping Dataset 2017: 3,421,083 orders, 206,209 users, 32.4M order lines. Reading order. 1) data checks, 2) retention curves, 3) basket-width lift (raw vs controlled), 4) what actually predicts retention, 5) milestone economics, 6) limitations.

206,209 users loaded

2. Weekly retention curves¶

The public data has no calendar dates, only days_since_prior_order, so cohorts are defined on each user's own clock (weeks since their 3rd order). Two caveats are visible in the curve:

  • days_since_prior_order is capped at 30, so every gap of 30+ days lands at exactly day 30 and produces the spikes at weeks 5 and 9. These are artefacts.
  • Every user has ≥4 orders, so everyone "returns" at least once by construction. All lifts here are compressed relative to a real-world population.

3. Basket width: raw lift vs controlled lift¶

Exposure = number of distinct departments (excluding the catch-all missing and other) across a user's first 3 orders. Outcome = repeat orders after order 3, so exposure and outcome never overlap.

4. What does predict retention: early cadence¶

Users who reorder within a week in their first three orders go on to place 3.2x the repeat orders of users who take more than two weeks. This is an association (fast reorderers are probably simply heavier grocery buyers), but it is the strongest early signal in the data.

cadence_tier users repeat_orders p_reach_20
0 fast (<=7d) 48028 25.012 0.498
1 medium (8-14d) 52623 14.973 0.336
2 slow (>14d) 105558 7.704 0.117

5. Free delivery on the 5th order: economics¶

Unit economics are assumptions, not data: the public set has no prices, margins or delivery costs. Everything is expressed as a fraction of average order value (AOV), so swap in First Club's real numbers in src/assumptions.py.

Break-even lift L* is where incremental contribution equals the fee waived:
L* = fee% × P(reach 5th order) / (baseline orders in 90 days × contribution per order%)

{
  "contribution_per_order": 0.21,
  "users_per_arm": 7333,
  "abs_delta_orders": 0.2524803198973579,
  "assumptions": {
    "gross_margin_pct": 0.25,
    "fulfilment_cost_pct": 0.1,
    "delivery_fee_pct": 0.06,
    "horizon_days": 90
  }
}
segment users p_reach_order5 mean_orders_90d sd_orders_90d break_even_lift
0 all users 206209 0.884 5.488 5.457 0.046
1 slow (>14d) 105558 0.834 3.510 3.177 0.068
2 medium (8-14d) 52623 0.922 5.806 4.276 0.045
3 fast (<=7d) 48028 0.950 9.486 7.805 0.029
4 width 1-3 departments 21446 0.873 5.354 5.757 0.047
5 width 4+ departments 184763 0.885 5.504 5.421 0.046

Targeting. Break-even lift is lowest for fast reorderers (they have the most orders to gain from, and almost all reach order 5 anyway) and highest for slow users. But fast users also include the most deadweight (they would have hit order 5 regardless). The data cannot separate those effects; an experiment can.

Experiment sizing. To detect the base-case break-even lift (+0.25 orders per user over 90 days, SD 5.46) at 5% significance and 80% power needs about 7,300 users per arm.

6. Limitations¶

  • No calendar dates, so no seasonality and no true acquisition cohorts.
  • days_since_prior_order capped at 30; gaps ≥30 days are indistinguishable.
  • Only users with 4-100 orders are included, which truncates retention at both ends.
  • Associations, not causal effects. Break-even economics rely on illustrative cost inputs.
  • The 6% break-even is not a data result: it needs fee ≈ 6% of AOV with contribution ≈ 16%, or fee ≈ 8% with ≈ 21%.
